opus-5.5.text:
I think there's a fairly direct link, actually. With ShinkaEvolve, the whole point was sample efficiency. A lot of these LLM-driven evolutionary systems, if you look at something like AlphaEvolve, need thousands of program evaluations to find a good solution. We were able to get state-of-the-art circle packing results with something like a few hundred. And we did that by being smarter about which parent programs to sample, by rejecting candidates that are too similar to things we've already tried, and by using a bandit to choose which LLM to ask for each mutation.

Now think about ARC AGI. Each task is its own little search problem. You have a handful of input-output examples and you need to find the program, or the transformation, that explains them. If every task costs you thousands of LLM calls, you simply can't afford to run open-ended search across the whole benchmark. And there are compute limits on the competition side as well. So efficiency isn't just a nice extra. It's what decides whether you can do this kind of search at all.

The other point is that efficiency gives you room to explore. If each step is cheaper, you can spend the budget you save on more diverse hypotheses, on longer evolutionary runs, or on going back and refining things. ARC really rewards that, because the right abstraction is often something you only find after wandering through quite a few wrong ones. So for me, a more efficient system effectively becomes a more creative system at a fixed budget.

And there's a longer-term angle too. If the search is cheap enough, you can start doing meta-level things: evolving the prompts, the mutation operators, maybe even the search strategy itself, and carrying what you learned on one task over to the next. That kind of accumulation is, I think, much closer to what ARC is really trying to measure, which is how efficiently you acquire new skills, not just raw performance. So in a way, making Shinka more efficient is aligned with the spirit of the benchmark itself.

r001.rationale: The response says efficiency enables more diverse hypotheses and longer search runs, but it does not identify scaling up instruction generation.

r002.rationale: The response links efficient search and broader exploration to ARC, but does not propose generating more instructions through Shinka’s open-ended search as a way to improve performance.

r003.rationale: The response mentions ARC input-output examples, but not that they provide a predictive signal for final test performance or serve as a condition for continued open-ended search.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there are really two sides to this. The first is almost mechanical: Shinka, like any evolutionary program-search system, is fundamentally bottlenecked by how many candidate programs you can generate, evaluate, and feed back into the loop within a fixed compute budget. Every token you spend on a verbose, redundant mutation, every evaluation you run on a program that was never going to work, is a sample you didn't get to spend somewhere more promising. So efficiency isn't just about saving money, it directly translates into more iterations of the search, a larger and more diverse population, and more chances to stumble into the kind of insight that actually cracks a task.

And ARC is exactly the sort of benchmark where that matters, because the tasks are sparse. You get a handful of demonstration pairs and you have to infer a rule that is often quite non-obvious. There's no gradient to follow. It's essentially a discrete search over hypotheses, and the thing that separates solving a task from not solving it is often whether you happened to explore the right region of program space before you ran out of budget. So if I can make each step cheaper, I can afford to be more exploratory, try more weird ideas, keep more lineages alive instead of greedily collapsing onto the first thing that partially works.

The second side is more subtle and, honestly, the one I find more interesting. Efficiency pressure forces you to be smarter about *how* you search, not just how much. When you can't afford brute force, you start asking: which parent programs are actually worth mutating? Can the model reason about why a previous attempt failed rather than just proposing something random? Can we reuse partial solutions or abstractions across tasks instead of starting from scratch each time? Those are the mechanisms that make the search less like a lottery and more like something that resembles reasoning. And I think that's ultimately what ARC is probing for. So the constraint ends up being a design signal. It pushes the system toward the kind of structured, cumulative search that I suspect is what you actually need to make progress, as opposed to just throwing more samples at it.

r001.rationale: The response says efficiency allows Shinka to generate and evaluate more candidate programs within the same compute budget, scaling up its search generation.

r002.rationale: It proposes that more exploratory program search and more chances to find a useful idea could improve performance on ARC tasks.

r003.rationale: The response discusses ARC demonstrations as sparse examples, but does not say they provide a predictive signal for final test performance or condition continued search on that signal.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that efficiency buys you more experimentation. With something like Shinka, you’re searching over programs, evaluating them, and using that feedback to propose better candidates. If that loop becomes cheaper, you can explore more ideas within the same compute budget, or spend more effort refining the promising ones.

For ARC AGI, that could be particularly useful because you’re trying to infer a rule from just a handful of examples. Your first hypothesis might explain two examples but fail on the third. Being able to quickly test and revise different hypotheses gives you more chances to find a program that captures the underlying transformation.

But it’s not automatic. You can also become very efficient at finding programs that fit the demonstrations without generalizing. So the opportunity is to use that efficiency for a broader, more diverse search, alongside a good way of selecting which solutions to trust.

r001.rationale: The response says efficiency enables more program searches and experimentation, but does not identify scaling up Shinka’s instruction generation.

r002.rationale: It connects broader hypothesis search with finding ARC solutions, but does not say that generating more instructions through Shinka’s open-ended search may improve performance.

r003.rationale: It discusses testing hypotheses against examples and warns that fitting demonstrations may not generalize, but does not identify the examples as a predictive signal for final test performance that conditions continued progress through open-ended search.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main connection is that efficiency lets you do more search. With something like Shinka, you're proposing changes to a program, evaluating them, and using that feedback to decide what to try next. If you can make that loop cheaper and faster, you can explore more candidates and go through more rounds of improvement within the same compute budget.

For ARC, that could mean trying more hypotheses about the transformation behind a task, checking them against the examples, and refining the promising ones. You don't necessarily need a better initial proposal if you can afford to test and improve many more proposals.

Of course, that only helps if the feedback is useful. You can also become very efficient at fitting the few examples without discovering a rule that generalizes. So efficiency gives you more opportunities to find a good solution; how you evaluate and guide that search is what turns those opportunities into better performance.

r001.rationale: The response says a cheaper, faster search loop allows Shinka to explore more candidates and complete more rounds within the same compute budget, communicating scaled-up generation.

r002.rationale: It proposes trying more ARC task hypotheses, testing and refining them, and says this can lead to better performance.

r003.rationale: The response warns that feedback may encourage overfitting and says useful evaluation matters, but it does not state that ARC training examples predict final test performance as a condition for continued progress.
